claim: 294 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidates are currently being evaluated.
source: There is an unprecedented effort for SARS-CoV-2 vaccine development with 294 candidates currently evaluated (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2021

claim: Variants of concern emerged before vaccine coverage was large enough to control the pandemic.
source: However, variants of concern have emerged before the vaccine coverage was large enough to control the pandemics (Cobey et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cobey et al., 2021

claim: Variants of concern might compromise the efficacy of current vaccines.
source: Despite a high rate of vaccine protection, these variants might compromise the efficacy of current vaccines (Kuzmina et al., 2021; Planas et al., 2021; Lustig et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on variant effects on vaccine efficacy

claim: Binding antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 are clearly associated with protection.
source: Binding antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 and in vitro neutralization of virus infection are clearly associated with protection (Khoury et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020; Earle et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating association between binding antibodies and protection

claim: In vitro neutralization of virus infection is clearly associated with protection.
source: Binding antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 and in vitro neutralization of virus infection are clearly associated with protection (Khoury et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020; Earle et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating association between neutralization and protection

claim: The respective contribution of binding antibodies and neutralization to virus control in vivo remains unclear.
source: However, the respective contribution to virus control in vivo remains unclear (Zost et al., 2020), and many other immunological mechanisms may also be involved, including other antibody-mediated functions (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity [ADCC], antibody-dependent complement deposition [ADCD], antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis [ADCP]; Yu et al., 2020; Mercado et al., 2020; Tauzin et al., 2021), as well as T cell immunity (McMahan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zost et al., 2020

claim: Many other immunological mechanisms may be involved in protection, including ADCC, ADCD, ADCP, and T cell immunity.
source: However, the respective contribution to virus control in vivo remains unclear (Zost et al., 2020), and many other immunological mechanisms may also be involved, including other antibody-mediated functions (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity [ADCC], antibody-dependent complement deposition [ADCD], antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis [ADCP]; Yu et al., 2020; Mercado et al., 2020; Tauzin et al., 2021), as well as T cell immunity (McMahan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on various immune mechanisms

claim: Correlates of protection may vary between vaccine platforms.
source: Furthermore, CoP may vary between the vaccine platforms (Plotkin, 2013; Plotkin, 2020; Bradfute and Bavari, 2011; Dagotto et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on vaccine platforms

claim: Non-human primate studies offer a unique opportunity to evaluate early markers of protective response.
source: Non-human primate (NHP) studies offer a unique opportunity to evaluate early markers of protective response (Muñoz-Fontela, 2020; Eyal and Lipsitch, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Muñoz-Fontela, 2020 and Eyal and Lipsitch, 2021

claim: Challenge studies in NHP allow the evaluation of vaccine impact on viral dynamics in different tissue compartments from day 1 of virus exposure.
source: Challenge studies in NHP allow the evaluation of vaccine impact on the viral dynamics in different tissue compartments (upper and lower respiratory tract) from day 1 of virus exposure (Yu et al., 2020; Mercado et al., 2020; Corbett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to NHP challenge studies

claim: The study used 18 cynomolgus macaques aged 37-58 months (8 females and 13 males).
source: Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis), aged 37–58 months (8 females and 13 males).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1A caption and study design description

claim: 24-26 weeks post-infection with SARS-CoV-2, 12 animals were randomly assigned to two experimental groups.
source: 24–26 weeks post-infection with SARS-CoV-2, 12 of these animals were randomly assigned in two experimental groups.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1A caption describing study design

claim: The convalescent-vaccinated group received 200 µg of αCD40.RBD vaccine.
source: The convalescent-vaccinated group (n=6) received 200 µg of αCD40.RBD vaccine.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1A caption describing study design

claim: All animals were exposed to a total dose of 10^6 pfu of SARS-CoV-2 virus via the combination of intra-nasal and intra-tracheal routes.
source: Four weeks after immunization, all animals were exposed to a total dose of 106 pfu of SARS-CoV-2 virus via the combination of intra-nasal and intra-tracheal routes.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1A caption describing study design

claim: Viral dynamics were characterized by a peak of genomic RNA production 3 days post-infection in both tracheal and nasopharyngeal compartments.
source: The viral dynamics during the primary infections were characterized by a peak of genomic RNA (gRNA) production 3 days post-infection in both tracheal and nasopharyngeal compartments, followed by a decrease toward undetectable levels beyond day 15 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Viral load decreased toward undetectable levels beyond day 15 post-infection.
source: The viral dynamics during the primary infections were characterized by a peak of genomic RNA (gRNA) production 3 days post-infection in both tracheal and nasopharyngeal compartments, followed by a decrease toward undetectable levels beyond day 15 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Viral dynamics were blunted following the second challenge of convalescent animals compared to naïve animals.
source: Compared to this naïve group, viral dynamics were blunted following the second challenge of convalescent animals with the lowest viral load observed in vaccinated animals (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The lowest viral load was observed in vaccinated animals.
source: Compared to this naïve group, viral dynamics were blunted following the second challenge of convalescent animals with the lowest viral load observed in vaccinated animals (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: A specific inoculum compartment distinguishes the virus from the challenge inoculum and the virus produced de novo.
source: We completed the model by a compartment for the inoculum to distinguish between the injected virus (Vs) and the virus produced de novo by the host (Vi and Vni).
evidence: Description of novel model feature

claim: Viral exchange between the two compartments plays a negligible role in viral kinetics compared with viral clearance.
source: However, as described in the literature (Gonçalves et al., 2021; Ke et al., 2020; Pinky et al., 2021) and demonstrated by the additional modelling work in Appendix 1 'Model building', viral transport within the respiratory tract plays a negligible role in viral kinetics compared with viral clearance.
evidence: Supported by citations and additional modeling work in Appendix 1

claim: The viral infectivity was estimated at 0.95 × 10^-6 (CI95% [0.18 × 10^-6; 4.94 × 10^-6]) (copies/mL)^-1 day^-1 in naïve animals.
source: We estimated the viral infectivity at 0.95 × 10–6 (CI95% [0.18 × 10–6; 4.94 × 10–6]) (copies/mL)–1 day–1 in naïve animals, which is in the range of previously reported modelling results whether in the case of SARS-CoV-2 virus (Kim et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020) or influenza (Myers et al., 2021; Baccam et al., 2006).
evidence: Model parameter estimation from data

claim: The estimated viral infectivity is in the range of previously reported modelling results for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza.
source: We estimated the viral infectivity at 0.95 × 10–6 (CI95% [0.18 × 10–6; 4.94 × 10–6]) (copies/mL)–1 day–1 in naïve animals, which is in the range of previously reported modelling results whether in the case of SARS-CoV-2 virus (Kim et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020) or influenza (Myers et al., 2021; Baccam et al., 2006).
evidence: Comparison with literature values supported by citations

claim: The loss rate of infected cells was estimated at 1.04 (CI95% [0.79; 1.37]) day^-1, corresponding to a mean half-life of 0.67 day.
source: We found estimates of the loss rates of infected cells of 1.04 (CI95% [0.79; 1.37]) day–1, corresponding to a mean half-life of 0.67 day.
evidence: Model parameter estimation from data

claim: The estimated loss rate of infected cells is consistent with previously published results on SARS-CoV-2 showing mean values ranging from 0.60 to 2 day^-1.
source: This estimation was consistent with previously published results obtained on SARS-CoV-2 virus showing the mean value of this parameter ranging from 0.60 to 2 day–1 (i.e., half-life between 0.35 and 1.16 days) (Gonçalves et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021; Gonçalves et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020; Marc et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison with literature values supported by citations

claim: The eclipse phase was estimated at 3 day^-1.
source: The eclipse phase (3 day–1) was found similar to the values commonly used in the literature (Gonçalves et al., 2020; Marc et al., 2021; Myers et al., 2021; Baccam et al., 2006).
evidence: Model parameter estimation from data, consistent with literature

claim: The clearance of the inoculum was much higher (20 virions day^-1) compared to the clearance of the virus produced de novo (3 virions day^-1).
source: Here, we distinguished the clearance of the inoculum which was much higher (20 virions day–1) as compared to the clearance of the virus produced de novo (3 virions day–1).
evidence: Model parameter estimation from data

claim: The viral production by each infected cell was estimated to be higher in the nasopharyngeal compartment (12.1 × 10^3 virions cell^-1 day^-1) compared to the tracheal compartment (0.92 × 10^3 virions cell^-1 day^-1).
source: Furthermore, the viral production by each infected cells was estimated to be higher in the nasopharyngeal compartment (12.1 × 103 virions cell–1 day–1, CI95% [3.15 × 103; 46.5 × 103]) as compared to the tracheal compartment (0.92 × 103 virions cell–1 day–1, CI95% [0.39 × 103; 2.13 × 103]).
evidence: Model parameter estimation from data

claim: The viral production estimates are in agreement with the observation of intense production of viral particles by primary human bronchial epithelial cells in culture.
source: These estimations are in agreement with the observation of the intense production of viral particles by primary human bronchial epithelial cells in culture (Robinot et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison with literature supported by citation

claim: The αCD40.RBD vaccine reduced the infection of target cells in the trachea by 99.6% compared to the naïve group.
source: The αCD40.RBD vaccine reduced by 99.6% the infection of target cells in the trachea compared to the naïve group.
evidence: Model-based estimation of vaccine effect

claim: The estimated clearance of infected cells was 1.04 day^-1 in naïve macaques and increased by 80% (1.86 day^-1) in convalescent macaques vaccinated by αCD40.RBD or not.
source: The estimated clearance of infected cells was 1.04 day–1 (95% CI 0.75; 1.45) in naïve macaques. It was increased by 80% (1.86 day–1) in the convalescent macaques vaccinated by αCD40.RBD or not.
evidence: Model-based estimation of vaccine effect

claim: The model predicts a very early decrease of target cells and viral inoculum which fully disappeared from day 2 onward.
source: Hence, a very early decrease of the target cells (all cells expressing ACE2) as well as of the viral inoculum which fully disappeared from day 2 onward were predicted (Figure 2C).
evidence: Model predictions shown in Figure 2C

claim: The number of infected cells and infectious viral particles increased up to day 2 and then decreased in all three groups.
source: In the three groups, the number of infected cells as well as infectious viral particles increased up to day 2 and then decreased.
evidence: Model predictions shown in Figure 2C

claim: The viral dynamic was blunted in vaccinated animals leading to a predicted maximum number of infectious viral particles below the detection threshold.
source: We show that this viral dynamic was blunted in the vaccinated animals leading to a predicted maximum number of infectious viral particles in the nasopharynx and the trachea below the detection threshold (Figure 2C).
evidence: Model predictions shown in Figure 2C

claim: The number of target cells would be decreased by the infection in the naïve and convalescent groups, whereas it would be preserved in vaccinated animals.
source: The number of target cells would be decreased by the infection in the naïve and the convalescent groups, whereas it would be preserved in vaccinated animals.
evidence: Model predictions shown in Figure 2C

claim: RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition is sufficient to capture most of the effect of the groups on the infection of target cells.
source: We demonstrate that the RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition measure is sufficient to capture most of the effect of the groups on the infection of target cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Systematic screening of biomarkers shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The integration of RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition in the model explains the variability of the cell infection rate with greater certainty than the group of intervention, reducing the unexplained variability by 87% compared to 66%.
source: The integration of this marker in the model explains the variability of the cell infection rate with greater certainty than the group of intervention, reducing the unexplained variability by 87% compared to 66% (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of model fit shown in Supplementary file 1

claim: When taking into account RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition, the effect of the group of intervention was no longer significant.
source: Furthermore, when taking into account the information provided by the RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition assay, the effect of the group of intervention was no longer significant (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Supplementary file 1

claim: An increase of 10^3 AU of RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition is linked with an increase of 1.8% (95CI% [1.2%; 2.3%]) of the viral infectivity.
source: A positive dependence was found between the viral infectivity and the RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition measure, linking an increase of 103 AU of the marker, whether over time or between animals, with an increase of 1.8% (95CI% [1.2%; 2.3%]) of the viral infectivity (see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Supplementary file 4

claim: IgG-binding anti-RBD antibodies were positively associated with the increase of the loss of infected cells.
source: We retained the anti-RBD binding IgG Ab that were positively associated to the increase of the loss of infected cells.
evidence: Systematic screening of biomarkers

claim: A large part of the variation of the infection rate (71%) and loss rate of infected cells (60%) were captured by RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition and anti-RBD-binding Ab concentration.
source: A large part of the variation of the infection rate (71%) and loss rate of infected cells (60%) were captured by the two markers of CoP: the RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition and the anti-RBD-binding Ab concentration.
evidence: Statistical analysis of model fit

claim: Vaccinated animals presented from the first day of challenge an effective reproduction number below 1.
source: When looking at this effective reproduction number according to the groups, the vaccinated animal presented from the first day of challenge an effective R below 1 meaning that no propagation of the infection started within the host.
evidence: Model predictions shown in Figure 4D

claim: The threshold of RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition leading to control of within-host infection (R<1) was around 30,000 AU.
source: Then, we looked at the threshold of the markers of interest leading to the control of the within-host infection (as defined by R<1) which was around 30,000 AU for the RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition assay.
evidence: Model-based threshold estimation

claim: A decrease of more than 2 log10 of the inhibition capacity would have been necessary to impair the control of the within-host infection in vaccinated animals.
source: According to the observed value of ECL RBD in vaccinated animals (e.g., 66 AU in Figure 4E), a decrease of more than 2 log10 of the inhibition capacity (to reach 81,000 AU), due to variant of concern (VoC) or waning of immunity, would have been necessary to impair the control of the within-host infection.
evidence: Model-based prediction shown in Figure 4E

claim: A decrease of neutralizing activity could be compensated by an increase of cell death as measured by an increase of binding IgG anti-RBD.
source: Moreover, a decrease of the neutralizing activity (i.e., increased ECL) could be compensated by an increase of cell death as measured by an increase of binding IgG anti-RBD as a surrogate.
evidence: Model-based prediction

claim: In the two-component spike nanoparticle vaccine study, six animals were vaccinated and compared to four naïve animals.
source: In this study, six animals were vaccinated and compared to four naïve animals (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Study design description

claim: The two-component spike nanoparticle vaccine decreased the infectivity rate by 99% and increased the clearance of infected cells by 79%.
source: The good fit of the data (Figure 5C and D) allows for estimating the effect of the vaccine that appeared here also to decrease the infectivity rate (by 99%) and increase the clearance of the infected cells by 79%.
evidence: Model-based estimation shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: For the two-component spike nanoparticle vaccine, inhibition of RBD binding to ACE2 was identified as the best mechanistic CoP.
source: Looking at the best mechanistic CoP following the previously described strategy, we ended here again with the inhibition of RBD binding to ACE2 as measured by ECL RBD.
evidence: Systematic screening of biomarkers

claim: For the two-component spike nanoparticle vaccine, RBD-ACE2-binding inhibition explained around 71% of the infectivity rate variability, compared to 65% explained by the groups.
source: In fact, this marker measured at baseline before challenge fulfilled the three criteria: (i) it led to the best model in front of a model adjusted for group effect, (ii) it rendered the group effect non-significant, and (iii) it explained around 71% of the infectivity rate variability, compared to 65% of variability explained by the groups.
evidence: Statistical analysis of model fit

claim: For the mRNA-1273 vaccine study, a reduction of the infection rate by 97% was estimated but no additional effect was found.
source: We started from the same model as defined previously. We estimated a reduction of the infection rate by 97% but we did not find any additional effect.
evidence: Model-based estimation

claim: For the mRNA-1273 vaccine, neutralization measured on live cells with Luciferase marker explained only 15% of the variability of estimated viral infectivity, while 19% were explained by the groups.
source: Looking at potential mechanistic CoP, we retained neutralization as measured on live cells with Luciferase marker. Although this marker led to the best fit and replaced the group effect (which was non-significant after adjustment for the marker), it explained only 15% of the variability of estimated viral infectivity, while 19% were explained by the groups.
evidence: Statistical analysis of model fit

claim: Both protein-based vaccines lead to the blockade of new cell infection.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrated, based upon challenge studies in NHP vaccinated with two different protein-based vaccine platforms, that both vaccines lead to the blockade of new cell infection.
evidence: Summary of findings from two vaccine studies

claim: Neutralizing antibodies likely represent a consistent mechanistic correlate of protection across protein-based vaccine platforms.
source: Neutralizing antibodies likely represent a consistent mechanistic correlate of protection (mCoP).
evidence: Conclusion from analysis of two protein-based vaccines

claim: Mechanistic correlates of protection could change across vaccine platforms because mechanisms of action are different.
source: This could change across vaccine platforms especially because mechanisms of action are different.
evidence: Inference from comparison of different vaccine platforms

claim: The binding inhibition assay may be more relevant to use as a CoP than cell-culture neutralization assays.
source: Interestingly, we found the simpler and easier to standardize and implement binding inhibition assay may be more relevant to use as a CoP than cell-culture neutralization assays.
evidence: Comparison of assay performance in identifying CoP

claim: The model was able to capture the effect of vaccines on the reduction of the rate of infection of target cells and identified additional effects beyond neutralizing antibodies.
source: The model was able to capture the effect of the vaccines on the reduction of the rate of infection of target cells and identified additional effects of vaccines beyond neutralizing antibodies.
evidence: Summary of modeling results

claim: The additional effect of vaccines consisted of increasing the loss rate of infected cells which was better reflected by IgG-binding antibodies and CD8+ T-cell responses.
source: This latter consisted of increasing the loss rate of infected cells which was better reflected by the IgG-binding antibodies and CD8+ T-cell responses in the case of the CD40-targeting vaccine.
evidence: Systematic screening of biomarkers

claim: The role of ADCC in natural infection has been previously shown.
source: The role of ADCC in natural infection has been previously shown (Dufloo et al., 2021), ADCD in DNA vaccine recipients (Yu et al., 2020) and with Ad26 vaccine (Alter et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: ADCD has been shown in DNA vaccine recipients and with Ad26 vaccine.
source: The role of ADCC in natural infection has been previously shown (Dufloo et al., 2021), ADCD in DNA vaccine recipients (Yu et al., 2020) and with Ad26 vaccine (Alter et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Two protein-based vaccines exert an additional effect on infected cell death which relied on the level of IgG anti-RBD-binding antibodies.
source: Here, we extended significantly these data by modelling the viral dynamic, showing that two other protein-based vaccines exert an additional effect on infected cell death which relied on the level of IgG anti-RBD-binding antibodies especially for the CD40.RBD-targeting vaccine.
evidence: Model-based analysis of vaccine effects

claim: A 20-fold reduction of viral neutralization might not translate in 20-fold reduction of vaccine efficacy.
source: However, a 20-fold reduction of viral neutralization might not translate in 20-fold reduction of vaccine efficacy (Emary et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Emary et al., 2021

claim: When the level of neutralizing antibodies was below a protective threshold, the cellular immune response appeared to be critical.
source: In the context of natural immunity, when the level of neutralizing antibodies was below a protective threshold, the cellular immune response appeared to be critical (McMahan et al., 2021; Chandrashekar et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to McMahan et al., 2021 and Chandrashekar et al., 2020

claim: An improvement of infected cell destruction could help to control the within-host infection and is quantitatively feasible.
source: We showed with our model that an improvement of infected cell destruction could help to control the within-host infection and is quantitatively feasible.
evidence: Model-based prediction

claim: Control of viral replication is the key for reducing infectivity.
source: The control of viral replication is the key for reducing infectivity (Leung et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2021) as well as disease severity (Néant, 2021; Gutmann et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Control of viral replication is the key for reducing disease severity.
source: The control of viral replication is the key for reducing infectivity (Leung et al., 2020; Marks et al., 2021) as well as disease severity (Néant, 2021; Gutmann et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: A decrease of 4- to 20-fold in neutralization as described for variants of concern is not enough to compromise the control of viral replication in the context of CD40.RBD-targeting vaccine.
source: According to our non-linear model linking the neutralization to the viral replication, a decrease of 4- to 20-fold in neutralization as described for the variants of concern (Planas et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021) is not enough, especially in the context of the response to CD40.RBD-targeting vaccine, to compromise the control of viral replication.
evidence: Model-based prediction with citations to variant studies

claim: The conserved effectiveness of mRNA vaccines in humans infected by alpha or beta variants is consistent with the hypothesis that moderate decreases in neutralization do not compromise viral control.
source: The results showing a conserved effectiveness of mRNA vaccines in humans infected by the alpha or beta variants (Charmet et al., 2021), although a decrease of neutralization has been reported (Planas et al., 2021), are consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on variant effectiveness

claim: An increased capacity of virion production was found in nasopharynx compared to the trachea.
source: Notably, we found an increased capacity of virion production in nasopharynx compared to the trachea which could be explained by the difference in target cells according to the compartment (Travaglini et al., 2020).
evidence: Model-based estimation with citation to support biological explanation

claim: The increased virion production in nasopharynx could be explained by the difference in target cells according to the compartment.
source: Notably, we found an increased capacity of virion production in nasopharynx compared to the trachea which could be explained by the difference in target cells according to the compartment (Travaglini et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Travaglini et al., 2020

claim: The increased virion production in nasopharynx may also be the consequence of a different local immune response.
source: This result needs to be confirmed as it may also be the consequence of a different local immune response (Pizzorno et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Pizzorno et al., 2020

claim: The modelling framework contributes to the improvement of understanding of immunological concepts by adding a quantitative evaluation of the contributions of different mechanisms of control of viral infection.
source: This modelling framework contributes to the improvement of the understanding of the immunological concepts by adding a quantitative evaluation of the contributions of different mechanisms of control of viral infection.
evidence: Summary of contribution of the work

claim: The results may help to develop vaccines for 'hard-to-target pathogens' or to predict their efficacy in aging and particular populations.
source: In terms of acceleration of vaccine development, our results may help to develop vaccines for 'hard-to-target pathogens', or to predict their efficacy in aging and particular populations (Pollard and Bijker, 2021).
evidence: Speculation about potential applications with citation

claim: The results should help in choosing vaccine dose at early development as well as deciding if and when boosting vaccination is needed.
source: It should also help in choosing vaccine dose, for instance at early development (Rhodes et al., 2018) as well as deciding if and when boosting vaccination is needed in the face of waning protective antibody levels (Gaebler et al., 2021; Vanshylla et al., 2021), at least in NHP studies although the framework could be extended to human studies using mixed approaches of within and between hosts modelling (Goyal et al., 2022) providing that enough information is collected.
evidence: Speculation about potential applications with citations

claim: Cynomolgus macaques aged 37-66 months (18 females and 13 males) originating from Mauritian AAALAC certified breeding centers were used in the study.
source: Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis), aged 37–66 months (18 females and 13 males) and originating from Mauritian AAALAC certified breeding centers were used in this study.
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

claim: All animals were housed in IDMIT facilities under BSL2 and BSL-3 containment when necessary.
source: All animals were housed in IDMIT facilities (CEA, Fontenay-aux-roses), under BSL2 and BSL-3 containment when necessary (Animal facility authorization #D92-032-02, Préfecture des Hauts de Seine, France) and in compliance with European Directive 2010/63/EU, the French regulations and the Standards for Human Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, of the Office for Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW, assurance number #A5826-01, US).
evidence: Description of experimental conditions

claim: The protocols were approved by the institutional ethical committee 'Comité d'Ethique en Expérimentation Animale du Commissariat à l'Energie Atomique et aux Energies Alternatives' (CEtEA #44) under statement number A20-011.
source: The protocols were approved by the institutional ethical committee 'Comité d'Ethique en Expérimentation Animale du Commissariat à l'Energie Atomique et aux Energies Alternatives' (CEtEA #44) under statement number A20-011.
evidence: Description of ethical approval

claim: The study was authorized by the 'Research, Innovation and Education Ministry' under registration number APAFIS#24434-2020030216532863v1.
source: The study was authorized by the 'Research, Innovation and Education Ministry' under registration number APAFIS#24434-2020030216532863v1.
evidence: Description of regulatory approval

claim: The proportion of infectious virus (µ) was fixed at 1/1000 according to previous work.
source: That is the case of the proportion of infectious virus (µ) that has been fixed at 1/1000 according to previous work (Gonçalves et al., 2021) and additional work (results not shown) evaluating the stability of the model estimation according to the value of this parameter.
evidence: Model parameter fixed based on literature and additional analysis

claim: gRNA was defined as proportional to the free virus.
source: We assumed that gRNA and sgRNA were proportional to the free virus and the infected cells, respectively.
evidence: Model assumption based on biological and mathematical reasoning

claim: sgRNA was defined as proportional to the infected cells.
source: We assumed that gRNA and sgRNA were proportional to the free virus and the infected cells, respectively.
evidence: Model assumption based on biological and mathematical reasoning

claim: sgRNA is only transcribed in infected cells.
source: First, sgRNA is only transcribed in infected cells (Sawicki et al., 2007).
evidence: Biological fact supported by citation

claim: Describing sgRNA as proportional to infected cells helps overcome identifiability issues between the parameters β and P.
source: Second, as described by Miao et al., 2011, to overcome identifiability issues between the parameters β and P typically observed in target-cell limited models.
evidence: Mathematical reasoning supported by citation
